keySentence: Wendy told stories because stories were the most powerful magic she knew.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: In Neverland Wendy became the mother that the lost boys had always needed and never had before. Each night she tucked them into their underground beds and began the story that would carry them to sleep. She told them about brave children who did the right thing even when it was frightening and difficult. The lost boys had never had anyone who cared enough to shape their imaginations with beautiful words. Wendy understood that a story told at bedtime was a gift that would last far longer than morning. It would stay inside a child's mind and become part of how they understood the world around them. Wendy told stories because stories were the most powerful magic she knew.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: In Neverland, Wendy's most important role was not cooking or cleaning but storytelling at the end of each day. She had noticed that the lost boys became calmer and kinder and braver on the nights when she told good stories. She chose her stories carefully — tales of loyalty and courage and the importance of going home when you were needed. The boys absorbed these ideas not as lessons but as feelings, which meant they went far deeper and stayed much longer. Wendy had learned something about human nature that many adults spent their whole lives failing to understand properly. A person who is told what to think will forget it, but a person who feels something true will carry it always. Stories were the most reliable tool she possessed for helping these lost and untethered boys find their way. Wendy told stories because stories were the most powerful magic she knew.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Wendy Darling's role in Neverland illuminates something important about why human beings need stories at all. The lost boys were not unintelligent or unkind — they simply had no framework for understanding their own experience. Without stories, their days were a series of events that happened and then were gone without leaving anything behind. Wendy's nightly storytelling gave their experience a shape — a beginning and a middle and a meaning-bearing end. She was doing, in the most intuitive and informal way possible, what all great literature attempts to accomplish. She was helping people understand what it means to be human by giving them carefully constructed imaginative experiences. Peter could give the boys adventure but only Wendy could give them the stories that made adventure worth having. The deepest magic is not the transformation of matter but the transformation of experience into understanding and meaning. Wendy told stories because stories were the most powerful magic she knew.
